problem: AgriVLN handles simple agricultural VLN instructions but misunderstands complex ones. A2A instructions are deliberately noisy and contain speaking mistakes and vague end conditions. Training-based instruction translators such as VLN-Trans need laborious annotation and generalize poorly beyond their training data.
motivation: Agricultural robots still depend on manual operation or fixed rails, so language-driven navigation would help. A2A instructions imitate the casual speech of farm workers, which makes aligning language with vision hard for the decision-maker. The paper's observation is that polishing the instruction, rather than changing the navigator, may make it easier to follow.
key_idea: Insert a training-free, few-shot-prompted LLM instruction translator that rewrites noisy instructions into precise ones, using five principles, before the AgriVLN VLM decision-maker.
insight: Concrete, visually grounded end conditions matter most. Among single principles, Representational Movement (e.g. 'occupies all your camera view') gives the largest gain, SR 0.47 to 0.57 with NE 2.91 to 2.39 (Table 2). The other four principles add 0.02-0.04 SR each, and all five combined reach 0.63. The choice of translator LLM matters: Claude-3.7 (BERTScore 0.9105, more conservative) and DeepSeek-R1 (0.8980, more aggressive) both score below GPT-4.1, which the authors attribute to leftover noise or deleted semantics.
method: Instruction Translator T(.): a few-shot-prompted LLM takes the original instruction W plus system and user templates and outputs a translated instruction W' and a reasoning thought rho; it needs no training or annotation.

Five translation principles (system prompt): Inessential Removal, Errors Revision, High-Low Separation (separate high-level goal from low-level orders with a delimiter phrase), Representational Rotation (rotate until the target is in the horizontal center), Representational Movement (stop when the target occupies the whole camera view). Each is a description plus one example.
Prompt template: tau_sys = base description ⊕ five principles ⊕ input/output format restriction.
Decision-maker D(.): the AgriVLN base model (NavGPT-style with a Subtask List module), with a VLM prompted end-to-end on W' and the front RGB image I_t to output a low-level action and reasoning.
Episode termination: [STOP] is predicted, the predicted action sequence deviates from the ground-truth sequence by more than 4 s (following A2A), or the max time step is reached.
Translator LLM variants: GPT-4.1 (default), Claude-3.7-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1; BERTScore between original and translated instruction is used to characterize how aggressive the translation is.

setting.backbone: GPT-4.1 mini (VLM decision-maker, frozen, API) + GPT-4.1 (translator LLM, frozen, API)
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: FORWARD, LEFT ROTATE, RIGHT ROTATE, STOP
setting.simulator: A2A benchmark (continuous environment simulation, 1,560 episodes, 6 scene types)
setting.privileged: none (ground-truth action sequence is used only to determine the deviation-based early termination of an episode, following A2A)

numbers.extra: training-free few-shot prompting; the paper does not name an official split for A2A, so 'test' is a placeholder
numbers.evidence: Table 1 row 9, A2A columns: SR 0.63, NE 2.28, BERTScr. 0.9035

numbers_note: The paper reports only on A2A and does not name an official split. Low-complexity (subtask=2) and high-complexity (subtask>=3) portions are also reported for T-araVLN_g: low SR 0.80 / NE 1.41, high SR 0.46 / NE 3.22. Baselines and human results are omitted.
results: On A2A, T-araVLN with the GPT-4.1 translator reaches SR 0.63 and NE 2.28 m, versus AgriVLN's 0.47 and 2.91 m, and beats NavGPT (0.33), SIA-VLN (0.31) and DILLM-VLN (0.36) on SR. On the low-complexity portion SR rises from 0.58 to 0.80, close to human performance (0.93). Human performance overall is 0.87 SR.
limitations: The translator uses no visual features, so translation cannot be grounded in the scene.
The translator adds 0.8-2.5 s of reasoning time per instruction.
All LLMs and VLMs are accessed only through APIs, with no open-source models tested and no real-robot deployment; the high-complexity portion remains hard (SR 0.46).
